title: From a Rs 2,000 Bet on Grandma's Murukku to a Rs 580-Crore Snacks Empire
excerpt: Sweet Karam Coffee started in 2015 with grandmother Janaki Paati's recipes and newspaper pamphlets. It has served nearly 5 lakh customers and turned home chefs into cloud-kitchen entrepreneurs.
body:
• Sweet Karam Coffee, a South Indian snacks brand founded in 2015, is now valued at Rs 580 crore after starting with a Rs 2,000 investment and recipes from the founders' grandmother, Janaki Paati.
  • The brand was born on a rainy Diwali in 2015 when the founding families could not find murukku outside that tasted like their grandmother's, and began cooking from her recipes.
  • Demand doubled after the pandemic as hygiene awareness rose; the company says it has served nearly 5 lakh customers, with bestsellers including Mysore Pak, murukku, banana chips, podis and filter coffee.
  • The growth has turned home chefs — mostly women — into entrepreneurs: many quit daily jobs to run full-fledged cloud kitchens with their own staff to meet Sweet Karam Coffee's demand.

It began with a craving on a rainy Diwali in 2015. A family of foodies in Chennai missed their grandmother's home-style murukku, hunted through shops, and found only factory-made versions stripped of authentic taste. Eleven years later, that craving has become Sweet Karam Coffee — a South Indian snacks brand now valued at Rs 580 crore.

The founders — husband-wife duo Anand Bharadwaj and Nalini Parthiban, along with Srivatsan Sundararaman and Veera Raghavan — started with recipes from their grandmother Janaki Paati and a Rs 2,000 investment in a small room of their house, according to the Times of India. There was no venture capital, no marketing budget. The team distributed newspaper pamphlets themselves to win their first customers, starting with home chefs within the family; extended family members pitched in with door deliveries in the early days.

Memory as a business model

"Memory as a business model "Every Diwali, our grandmother used to meticulously make the jaangris, murukku and mysurpa."

"Every Diwali, our grandmother used to meticulously make the jaangris, murukku and mysurpa. As she was cooking, she used to narrate tales to her grandchildren and make them do odd jobs," Nalini Parthiban told the outlet. "That memory of squeezing the jangris with our grandma is what led us to quit our jobs and start SKC, which is today a million-dollar brand."

The thesis was simple: India's snack aisle was dominated by mass-manufactured products, while the recipes people actually craved lived in grandmothers' kitchens. Sweet Karam Coffee commercialised that gap — traditional sweets and savouries made the home way, at scale. Its bestsellers now include Mysore Pak, murukku and mixtures, banana chips, podis and rice mixes, Andhra avakkai and South Indian filter coffee.

The pandemic tailwind

The business turned a corner after the pandemic, when awareness around health and hygiene pushed consumers toward trusted, home-style food. Nalini said demand doubled in that period. According to the company's website, the brand has served nearly 5 lakh customers.

The growth has had a second-order effect on livelihoods. Many of the home chefs who cook for the brand — mostly women — have quit their daily jobs and set up full-fledged cloud kitchens with their own staff as demand for Sweet Karam Coffee products has soared. It is a quiet inversion of the usual startup story: instead of gig workers serving a platform, home kitchens became the platform.

Why it matters

Sweet Karam Coffee's rise mirrors a broader shift in India's food economy. Consumers are paying a premium for regional authenticity over national brands, and the "grandmother's recipe" has become one of the most bankable assets in Indian D2C food. For the diaspora, the brand is also a familiar name in the nostalgia economy — the same murukku-and-filter-coffee craving that built it in Chennai travels in every NRI's suitcase at Diwali.

The caution, as with any nostalgia brand, is scale: the promise is grandmother's taste, and the Rs 580-crore question is whether that promise survives the jump from home kitchens to cloud kitchens without becoming exactly the factory-made product it set out to replace.
